notes.text: Shalt feed — That is, rule them, and take care of them, as a shepherd doth of his sheep, Psalm lxxviii, 70, 71. This expression, he useth to admonish David, that he was not made a king to advance his own glory, but for the good of his people; whom he ought to rule with all tenderness, and to watch over with all diligence.
A league — Whereby David obliged himself to rule them according to God's laws; and the people promised obedience to him.

glossa.text: *And they came.* ((RAB.)) So all the nations come together to Christ, and as though caressing him they say: *We are thy bone and thy flesh:* when they love and venerate in him the incarnation which he took from our nature in the womb of the Virgin.

*The ancients.* ((ID.)) The prophets and the apostles run together to Christ with equal faith and devotion.

*And they anointed.* ((ID.)) David is said to have been anointed twice, and Christ took the sovereignty first among the Jews, afterwards among the Gentiles.
*And forty.* ((ID.)) It is asked: why are not forty years and six months reckoned in the sum? etc., *as far as* which consists of four tens, and signifies the perfection of times and of things.

*In Hierusalem.* The Hebrews hand down that Sem the son of Noe, whom they call Melchisedech, founded Salem. This city the Jebusaeans afterwards held, from whom it obtained the name Jebus. Thence Hierusalem, as it were Jebus Salem, afterwards by Solomon it was called Jerosolyma, as it were Jerosalomonia, which afterwards was called Aelia by Aelius Adrianus.

notes.text: The city — In Jerusalem. Mountain - In his holy mountain.
The joy — This is spoken prophetically, because the joyful doctrine of the gospel was to go from thence to all nations. The city - Of God, who justly calls himself a great king.

Known — By long experience. Palaces - Possibly he may point at the king's palace and the temple, which was the palace of the king of heaven; which two palaces God did in a singular manner protect, and by protecting them, protected the whole city and people.

The kings — Either those kings confederate against Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. xx, 1, or the Assyrian princes; whom they vain- gloriously called kings, Isaiah x, 8. Passed - In their march towards Jerusalem.
Saw it — They did only look upon it, but not come into it, nor shoot an arrow there - nor cast a bank against it, 2 Kings xix, 32. Marvelled - At the wonderful works wrought by God.
Fear — At the tidings of Tirhakah's coming against them, 2 Kings xix, 9, and at that terrible slaughter of their army, ver. 35.

Breakest — Thou didst no less violently and suddenly destroy these raging enemies of Jerusalem, than sometimes thou destroyest the ships at sea with a fierce and vehement wind, such as the eastern winds were in those parts.

Heard — The predictions of the prophets have been verified by the events. Establish - God will defend her in all succeeding ages. And so God would have done, if Jerusalem had not forsaken him, and forfeited his protection.
Thought — It hath been the matter of our serious and deep meditation, when we have been worshipping in thy temple.

So — Thou art acknowledged to be such an one as thou hast affirmed thyself to be in thy Word, God Almighty, or All- sufficient, the Lord of hosts, and a strong tower to all that trust in thee. Righteousness - Of righteous actions; by which thou discoverest thy holiness.
Judgments — Upon thine and their enemies.
Tell — He bids them mark well her towers, bulwarks, and palaces, with thankfulness to God, when they should find upon enquiry, that not one of them were demolished.

Tell it — That they may continue their praises to God for this mercy, by which they hold and enjoy all their blessings. The preface, ver. 1-4. We need not fear the wicked, ver. 5. They cannot by their riches save either their friends or themselves from death, ver. 6-10. They cannot secure happiness to themselves, either in this world or the world to come, ver. 11-14. He comforts good men against the fear of death, or of the prosperity of the wicked, ver. 15-20. To the chief musician, A psalm for the sons of Korah.

glossa.text: *In the holy mount,* etc. ((Ibid.)) This is that mountain, etc., *as far as* upon which the Church is founded.

*It is founded with the joy.* ((HIER.)) As if he should say, she who before was subject to curses, etc., *as far as* he himself is Christ, who through the universal Church spreads joys abroad. *Mount Sion, the sides.* ((AUG.)) Whosoever cleave to anyone are called his sides, etc., *as far as* likewise *from the north shall every evil be spread abroad,* etc.

*In the houses.* Or, in the degrees, that is, according to the degrees of merits, because in each one severally he will give the knowledge of himself. *When he shall receive her.* To be guarded, and what need is there? *For the kings against.* But seeing by faith, namely thus, that this city is so worthy, they wondered, etc.

*The kings.* ((AUG., CASS.)) The princes of the Jews. *Being gathered together.* By Herod inquiring the place of the nativity. *They came together.* Saying with one accord: *In Bethlehem of Juda according to the Scriptures.*

*Seeing.* The things which they had read in the prophets. *They wondered.* At so great glory, not lightly or idly. *But they were troubled.* For sin, and *They were moved.* To faith, and so great was the dread, that the body trembled.
*There pains as of a woman in labour,* Of penance, seeing thus; but:

*With a vehement spirit,* Of Herod. *Thou shalt break the ships of Tharsis.* Because, in Tharsus, the ships of Cilicia which were believed to have carried the Magi over into their own country, were broken by Herod. *Tharsis.* ((AUG.)) Cilicia is a region named from Tharsus, etc., *as far as* having run through all he concludes. Therefore:

*As we have heard. In the city of the Lord of hosts,* because there he appoints angels as guards. He repeats. *In the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God.* That is, the Catholic Church, lest the assembly of heretics usurp this name to itself. But lest it be thought temporal, he adds: *God hath founded it for ever.* Not for an hour, as before the tabernacle of Moses

*We have received, O God, thy mercy.* ((CASS.)) Giving thanks for the coming of Christ, he admonishes concerning the degrees of the Church that are to be distributed, through which the Saviour may be known. *In the midst of the temple.* Jerusalem: they are the more grievously accused, who despise him who was beheld in the midst of them. By this the incarnation of Christ is noted, who according as he is man was presented in the temple.

*The right hand.* ((CASS.)) On this side the just are placed.

((AUG.)) *We have received, O God.* In what order she was founded, or what we have heard and seen. *Of thy temple. ((Ibid.))* That is, of a people not receiving *sucipientis* mercy, who to many: so that no grains seem to be there, but nevertheless some, because according to the name. *According to the name.* ((CASS.)) Which is everywhere spread abroad, because there is none, even if he know not the worship, who does not submit himself to this name. *Or according to the name.* This is, as the reverence of thy name, etc., *as far as* thy propitiation hath justified many, who all praise thee.

*Let it be glad.* ((AUG.)) Although the just labour among thorns, etc., *as far as* it is theirs now to gather, God's to separate. *Mount Sion, and let them rejoice.* ((CASS.)) The Church, which is in the beholding of the people. *The daughters of Juda, because of thy judgments, O Lord.* Holy women. By Juda their nation is shown, which is on account of Christ, who is of Juda, and let these rejoice, that in both sexes the Church may be. ((AUG.)) The cause of gladness is the judgments to come, wherein they know that they shall come to blessedness. Let those who are within be glad; you who are without, encompass.

*Encompass.* By showing honours. *Embrace her.* With charity. *Tell in her towers. Set your hearts.* ((CASS.)) Preach to others in the concord of the Apostles, etc., *as far as* lest, being remiss through gladness, they grow slack.

*Her strength.* ((AUG.)) The strength of the city is charity, which nothing overcomes; whence Solomon: *Love is strong as death.* ((CASS.)) He admonishes to set the hearts on the strength of the Church. *Distribute her houses, that you may relate it in another generation.* That is, the offices distinguished, etc., *as far as* whom the Lord first chose.
*For this is,* etc. This is what must be related, a brief sentence, but one which concludes all things. *For ever,* against those who made temporal men gods.

notes.text: I knew a man in Christ — That is, a Christian. It is plain from 2 Cor. xii, 6, 7, that he means himself, though in modesty he speaks as of a third person. Whether in the body or out of the body I know not - It is equally possible with God to present distant things to the imagination in the body, as if the soul were absent from it, and present with them; or to transport both soul and body for what time he pleases to heaven; or to transport the soul only thither for a season, and in the mean time to preserve the body fit for its re- entrance. But since the apostle himself did not know whether his soul was in the body, or whether one or both were actually in heaven, it would be vain curiosity for us to attempt determining it. The third heaven - Where God is; far above the aerial and the starry heaven. Some suppose it was here the apostle was let into the mystery of the future state of the church; and received his orders to turn from the Jews and go to the gentiles.
Yea, I knew such a man — That at another time.

He was caught up into paradise — The seat of happy spirits in their separate state, between death and the resurrection. Things which it is not possible for man to utter - Human language being incapable of expressing them. Here he anticipated the joyous rest of the righteous that die in the Lord. But this rapture did not precede, but follow after, his being caught up to the third heaven: a strong intimation that he must first discharge his mission, and then enter into glory. And beyond all doubt, such a foretaste of it served to strengthen him in all his after trials, when he could call to mind the very joy that was prepared for him.
Of such an one I will — I might, glory; but I will not glory of myself - As considered in myself.

For if I should resolve to glory — Referring to, I might glory of such a glorious Revelation. I should not be a fool - That is, it could not justly be accounted folly to relate the naked truth. But I forbear - I speak sparingly of these things, for fear any one should think too highly of me - O where is this fear now to be found? Who is afraid of this?

There was given me — By the wise and gracious providence of God. A thorn in the flesh - A visitation more painful than any thorn sticking in the flesh. A messenger or angel of Satan to buffet me - Perhaps both visibly and invisibly; and the word in the original expresses the present, as well as the past, time. All kinds of affliction had befallen the apostle. Yet none of those did he deprecate. But here he speaks of one, as above all the rest, one that macerated him with weakness, and by the pain and ignominy of it prevented his being lifted up mere, or, at least, not less, than the most vehement head ache could have done; which many of the ancients say he laboured under. St. Paul seems to have had a fresh fear of these buffetings every moment, when he so frequently represses himself in his boasting, though it was extorted from him by the utmost necessity.
Concerning this — He had now forgot his being lifted up. I besought the Lord thrice - As our Lord besought his Father.

But he said to me — ln answer to my third request. My grace is sufficient for thee - How tender a repulse! We see there may be grace where there is the quickest sense of pain. My strength is more illustriously displayed by the weakness of the instrument. Therefore I will glory in my weaknesses rather than my Revelations, that the strength of Christ may rest upon me - The Greek word properly means, may cover me all over like a tent. We ought most willingly to accept whatever tends to this end, however contrary to flesh and blood.
Weaknesses — Whether proceeding from Satan or men. For when I am weak - Deeply conscious of my weakness, then does the strength of Christ rest upon me.

glossa.text:
*I know a man.* As if concerning another, both the thing is told, and boasting is avoided. *Whether in the body, or,* etc. This the Apostle did not know, whether, when he was caught up, the soul was in the body, or whether it went out of the body altogether, so that the body lay dead, or whether, according to some other manner of a living body wherein the soul was, his mind was taken up to see or to hear the unspeakable things of that vision. And because this was uncertain, therefore perhaps he said, *whether in the body, or without. Caught up.* Lifted up against nature.

*Even unto the third heaven.* That is, unto the knowledge of the Godhead. The first heaven is the airy; the second, the firmament; the third spiritual, where the angels and the holy souls enjoy the contemplation of God.

*He was caught up. ((THEOPH.))* See his utmost lowliness and humility, how he recounts these things as though of another: for of such a one, he says, I will glory. But for whose sake (if it was another that was caught up) dost thou glory? And so he says these things of himself. *Secret words.* An intimation concerning the hidden essence of God, as it were through words.
*Above that which,* etc. For if I should relate great things and many, perhaps some would think that I am not weak, but an immortal man, or an angel, etc.; and therefore I speak sparingly of myself.

*And lest the greatness.* I forbear to glory much, lest I be thought to be other than I am. And therefore a sting was given, pricking the flesh. Who? A malignant angel sent by Satan, that he might buffet him, that is, might repress every motion of pride by striking in tribulations, or by tempting (as some say) through lust. But a temptation to which consent is not given is not a sin, but matter for the exercise of virtue.

*He said to me.* By inspiration, or by an angel. *For power is made perfect in infirmity.* That is the perfection of virtues which has a contrary infirmity, with which it may lawfully strive: and therefore I will glory in infirmities, not unwillingly, but gladly.

notes.text: Matt. xiii, 54; Luke iv, 16.
Is not this the carpenter? — There can be no doubt, but in his youth he wrought with his supposed father Joseph.

He could do no miracle there — Not consistently with his wisdom and goodness. It being inconsistent with his wisdom to work them there, where it could not promote his great end; and with his goodness, seeing he well knew his countrymen would reject whatever evidence could be given them. And therefore to have given them more evidence, would only have increased their damnation.
He marvelled — As man. As he was God, nothing was strange to him.
Matt. x, 1; Luke ix, 1.

He commanded them to take nothing for their journey — That they might be always unincumbered, free, ready for motion. Save a staff only - He that had one might take it; but he that had not was not to provide one, Matt. x, 9. Luke ix, 3.

Be shod with sandals — As you usually are. Sandals were pieces of strong leather or wood, tied under the sole of the foot by thongs, something resembling modern clogs. The shoes which they are in St. Matthew forbidden to take, were a kind of short boots, reaching a little above the mid-leg, which were then commonly used in journeys. Our Lord intended by this mission to initiate them into their apostolic work. And it was doubtless an encouragement to them all their life after, to recollect the care which God took of them, when they had left all they had, and went out quite unfurnished for such an expedition. In this view our Lord himself leads them to consider it, Luke xxii, xxxv, When I sent you forth without purse or scrip, lacked ye any thing?
Matt. x, 11; Luke ix, 4.
Luke ix, 6.

They anointed with oil many that were sick — Which St. James gives as a general direction, James v, 14, 15, adding those peremptory words, And the Lord shall heal him - He shall be restored to health: not by the natural efficacy of the oil, but by the supernatural blessing of God. And it seems this was the great standing means of healing, desperate diseases in the Christian Church, long before extreme unction was used or heard of, which bears scarce any resemblance to it; the former being used only as a means of health; the latter only when life is despaired of.

glossa.text: *Whence hath this man,* etc. Wonderful blindness. In his deeds and in his words they are able to know Christ, for the mere knowledge of his stock they despise him.
*A craftsman. ((BEDA.))* He who works with fire and with spirit; whence: *He shall baptize you in fire and in spirit ((Joan. I))* . He is the craftsman who crafted the dawn and the sun.

*A prophet is not without honour.* It is well-nigh natural that fellow-citizens should envy fellow-citizens, because they remember not his works but the childhood which they saw.

((ISID.)) Meanness often attends a man's origin. As, *Who is the son of Isai ((III Reg. XII))*. But: *The Lord beholdeth the lowly, and the high he knoweth afar off ((Psal. CXXXVII))*.

*And he could not,* etc. Lest by doing many mighty works he should condemn the worse his unbelieving fellow-citizens. Or because he is despised in his own country, he did few mighty works and signs there, lest they should be wholly excusable. Greater signs he does daily among the Gentiles, not so much in the healing of bodies as of souls.
*And he wondered. ((BEDA.))* Not as at something unforeseen, but he shows it as a thing to be wondered at, because they believe neither the prophets, nor him whom they behold present.

*And he called. ((HIER.))* The twelve apostles are sent, and there is given them power, precepts of teaching, that word and deed together may accompany them: and that mighty works may be mingled with invisible promises, and so, when they anoint the sick with oil, they strengthen the weakness of faith by a mighty work.

*And he gave them,* etc. The kind Lord and master does not grudge his own power to his disciples and servants. But he acts by his own power, they by their own weakness, if they do anything, and they confess the Lord's might, saying: *In the name of Jesus arise and walk ((Act. III))*.

*That they should take nothing,* etc. Let their confidence in the Lord be so great that they may know most certainly that nothing is wanting, lest, while they provide temporal things for themselves, they provide eternal things the less for others.

 ((BEDA.)) Matthew and Luke record that the Lord said to his disciples that they should not carry even a staff: Mark, that they should take nothing save a staff. But they take the staff really. Mark understands by the staff the power of receiving what is necessary from those subject to them.

*Shod with sandals. ((ID.))* That the foot be neither covered nor bare to the ground, that is, that neither the Gospel be hidden, nor lean upon earthly advantages.

*That they should not put on two coats. ((ID.))* Which is, that they should walk in singleness, not in doubleness.

*Shake off the dust from your feet. ((ID.))* The dust is shaken off from the feet in testimony of their labour, that they have entered the city, that the preaching has reached even unto them. Or that they have received nothing from them toward the food that was needful, who despised the Gospel.

*And they anointed with oil. ((ID.))* James says: *Is any man sick among you? let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil ((Jac. V))*, etc. Whence it is plain that this custom was handed down from the apostles, that the possessed and other sick persons should be anointed with oil consecrated by a bishop.

notes.text: And — He that sat upon the throne, Jesus Christ. Son of man - A phrase which is ninety-five times, at least, used in this prophecy to keep him humble who had such great Revelations. Stand - Arise, fear not. And with this command God sent forth a power enabling him to rise and stand.
The spirit — The same spirit which actuated the living creatures.
Shall know — They that obey shall know by the good I will do them, those that will not, by the evil which I will bring upon them.

Look — For supply of their wants, and for help and defense against their oppressors. Until - Until he help and save us. David describes the danger he and his people had been in, ver. 1-5. Blesses God for delivering them, ver. 6-8. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text: *To thee have I lifted up.* ((ID.)) First the voice of the troubled looking to God, not to other patronages; secondly, he prays for mercy against those who insult him. ((AUG.)) *To thee have I lifted up.* Whither should he lift them, save whither he tended in ascending? this man does not regard himself, as the proud man does who pleases himself: for he who is displeasing to himself, such a one pleases God; and he to whom God is pleasing is himself displeasing to himself. *I have lifted up.* The ascent therefore is in the affection, etc., *as far as* but he who is a pilgrim and desires his country.

*Behold as the eyes,* etc. ((CASS.)) The servant lifts his eyes to the hands of his master, when he is in want or when he is beaten, because both are in the master's power. *As the eyes of the handmaid.* ((AUG.)) *The servant* is the people; *the Lord,* Christ; *the handmaid,* the Church; the mistress, the power of God and the wisdom of God. And though we are now sons and friends by grace, yet we are servants by creation, because every creature serves God. ((CASS.)) He gives a similitude *similttudinem* from the manservant and the handmaid, the master and the mistress, lest the feminine and weaker sex suppose itself excepted.

*Have mercy.* ((ID.)) The second part, where he prays for mercy against those who insult him. The servant who is beaten, having lifted his eyes to God, breaks forth into the needful cry: *Have mercy.*

*We are filled.* As when it is said: What dost thou believe, madman; dost thou see what thou believest? Has anyone returned from the dead, and told thee what is done there? Behold, what I love, I see and enjoy.

((ISID.)) Meanness often attends a man's origin. As, *Who is the son of Isai ((III Reg. XII))*. But: *The Lord beholdeth the lowly, and the high he knoweth afar off ((Psal. CXXXVII))*.

*And he could not,* etc. Lest by doing many mighty works he should condemn the worse his unbelieving fellow-citizens. Or because he is despised in his own country, he did few mighty works and signs there, lest they should be wholly excusable. Greater signs he does daily among the Gentiles, not so much in the healing of bodies as of souls.
*And he wondered. ((BEDA.))* Not as at something unforeseen, but he shows it as a thing to be wondered at, because they believe neither the prophets, nor him whom they behold present.

*And he called. ((HIER.))* The twelve apostles are sent, and there is given them power, precepts of teaching, that word and deed together may accompany them: and that mighty works may be mingled with invisible promises, and so, when they anoint the sick with oil, they strengthen the weakness of faith by a mighty work.

*And he gave them,* etc. The kind Lord and master does not grudge his own power to his disciples and servants. But he acts by his own power, they by their own weakness, if they do anything, and they confess the Lord's might, saying: *In the name of Jesus arise and walk ((Act. III))*.

*That they should take nothing,* etc. Let their confidence in the Lord be so great that they may know most certainly that nothing is wanting, lest, while they provide temporal things for themselves, they provide eternal things the less for others.

 ((BEDA.)) Matthew and Luke record that the Lord said to his disciples that they should not carry even a staff: Mark, that they should take nothing save a staff. But they take the staff really. Mark understands by the staff the power of receiving what is necessary from those subject to them.

*Shod with sandals. ((ID.))* That the foot be neither covered nor bare to the ground, that is, that neither the Gospel be hidden, nor lean upon earthly advantages.

*That they should not put on two coats. ((ID.))* Which is, that they should walk in singleness, not in doubleness.

*Shake off the dust from your feet. ((ID.))* The dust is shaken off from the feet in testimony of their labour, that they have entered the city, that the preaching has reached even unto them. Or that they have received nothing from them toward the food that was needful, who despised the Gospel.

*And they anointed with oil. ((ID.))* James says: *Is any man sick among you? let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil ((Jac. V))*, etc. Whence it is plain that this custom was handed down from the apostles, that the possessed and other sick persons should be anointed with oil consecrated by a bishop.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised.
In the city of our God, on the holy mountain.
He sent them out two by two, with nothing for the road.
No bread, no bag, only the Word and one another.
A prophet is honored everywhere but at home.
Still we will go where Christ would send us.
Come, let us worship; then come, let us be sent.
We come to praise, and we will go. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Walk about Zion, count her towers, feel the ground under your feet; this is the city of our God, and God is its sure defense.
Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised.
Jesus calls the twelve and sends them down the road two by two, taking nothing but a staff: no bread, no bag, no money in their belts.
Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised.
Even at home they would not believe him, and he marveled, yet he kept sending, kept healing, kept calling unlikely people to go.
Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised.
So worship now, and then lace up your sandals; the same Lord who gathers us here will send us out light and unafraid.
Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised, and we will go.
